extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of history/philosophy of science; historians and practicing scientists interested in scientific method and discovery
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes criteria for evaluating or producing scientific inquiry and scientific writings (induction vs hypothesis, role of mathematics, experiment design, and editorial/publishing formulation of controversial hypotheses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere induction (enumeratio simplex) is incompetent
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere induction, 'enumeratio simplex', is spoken of by Bacon with contempt as utterly incompetent: a thousand instances may be contradicted by the thousand and first, so that no enumeration of instances, however large, is 'sure demonstration' while any are left.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat large unstructured collections of instances as proof. Enumeration alone cannot deliver 'sure demonstration'; additional structure (e.g., hypothesis, special object, or deductive framework) is required. The text uses this to reject Baconian faith in simple enumeration as a route to scientific truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observational programs must have a 'special object'
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism (via M. Biot) of meteorological observatories: they have produced 'nothing' because 'there is no special object' — systematic mass observation without a clearly defined aim yields little.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design observational campaigns around a clear 'special object' or targeted hypothesis. Avoid open-ended mass-data collection without an articulated theoretical goal, otherwise risk accumulating 'millions of useless observations.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis-driven discovery (few facts suggest hypothesis; then deduce and test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern discoveries arise from a few facts that suggest an hypothesis; the necessary results of that supposition are worked out and then other facts are examined to see if the consequences are found in nature. The 'trial of the hypothesis' is the 'special object.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize formulation of plausible hypotheses from sparse data, derive testable consequences, then seek targeted observations/experiments. Recognize that inventing hypotheses depends on sagacity rather than a mechanical rule. The history of discovery (Kepler → Newton example) exemplifies this route.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematics is the great instrument of exact inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Sir John Herschel: 'sound and sufficient knowledge of mathematics, the great instrument of all exact inquiry, without which no man can ever make such advances ... as can entitle him to form an independent opinion.' Bacon undervalued mathematics and treated it as handmaid rather than instrument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure sufficient mathematical competence to operate in higher departments of science; mathematical deduction frequently supplies necessary methods for forming and testing hypotheses (e.g., Newton's use of mathematics to deduce consequences of inverse-square law).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conflate deduction with observation ('observare re' vs 'observare mente')
rubrics_metrics.description: Bacon's phrasing linked observation 'in fact' and 'in thought', but Bacon did not include deduction under observation. The text emphasizes that mathematical deduction should not be reckoned as the same sort of thing as empirical observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep observational data distinct from deductive/mathematical reasoning when describing methods. Recognize the complementary roles: observations supply facts; deduction/mathematics derive consequences to be tested against facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical discovery may require conceiving laws not previously thought
rubrics_metrics.description: The physical philosopher must sometimes 'conceive law which never was in his previous thought — to educe the unknown, not to choose among the known.' Bacon's method, which the author reads as choosing among known alternatives, is therefore inadequate in many cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methods and evaluation should allow for the generation of genuinely novel explanatory laws, not only selection among a predefined menu of hypotheses. Be skeptical of procedures that presuppose all candidate laws are already conceived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design experiments to include critical variations that can falsify theories
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: Bacon's windmill experiment 'overlooks an obvious circumstance which makes the experiment inconclusive, and an equally obvious variation ... would have shown him that his theory was false.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constructing experiments, include control/variant conditions that would clearly falsify the hypothesis if it were false. Avoid experimental designs that leave obvious alternative explanations untested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Large collections of facts are useful primarily for testing theories, not for inventing them
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrast: Bacon thought large collections of facts lead to theory; the history of discovery shows a few facts suggest an hypothesis which is then tested. 'What are large collections of facts for? To make theories from, says Bacon: to try ready-made theories by, says the history of discovery.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mass observations to refine and test theoretical proposals rather than expecting unguided accumulation to produce discovery. Plan data collection with the intention of adjudicating between theoretical predictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formulation and presentation of controversial scientific claims as 'hypothesis' not 'assertion' (Copernicus corrections)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Congregation of the Index required corrections to Copernicus: present Earth's motion 'per hypothesis' rather than as asserted fact; change chapter headings from 'demonstration' to 'hypothesis'; avoid language that asserts conformity or conflict with Scripture; do not call the Earth a 'star'; prefer 'assume' to 'acknowledge.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When publishing controversial theories in sensitive contexts, phrase them as hypotheses and avoid categorical assertions that claim definitive demonstration. More generally, be careful in terminology: 'assume'/'hypothesis' vs 'assert'/'demonstration' — wording affects reception and censorship risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of sagacity in hypothesis generation is not codifiable
rubrics_metrics.description: The inventor of hypothesis, if pressed, cannot lay out a rule-based method; the creative jump is akin to Zerah Colburn's 'God put it into my head'—generation of hypotheses depends on unformulable sagacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge limits of formal method: expect and allow for individual insight and creative leaps in hypothesis formation. Evaluation should not demand a fully formalized recipe for hypothesis generation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensive knowledge of prior mathematical and scientific work is essential
rubrics_metrics.description: Bacon's ignorance of contemporary mathematics (Napier's logarithms, Kepler's calculations, Archimedes, etc.) led him to undervalue mathematics and to propose inquiries already addressed; this impaired the practical value of his method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before proposing methods or experiments, survey existing literature and mathematical advances. Failure to account for prior work risks duplicating errors or overlooking tools that materially change method and feasibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bacon's method is more valuable for preventing error than for facilitating discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: The author characterizes Bacon as 'eminently the philosopher of error prevented, not of progress facilitated' — his rules and refutations help eliminate mistakes but do less to generate successful discoveries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Baconian-style rules and fallacy refutations primarily as checks against error in experimental reasoning and interpretation, while relying on hypothesis-driven, mathematically informed approaches to actively facilitate discovery.
